command.def: One line typed into the shell: a program name followed by its arguments, such as `python 02_collect_events.py`.
levels: A command is like telling a robot exactly one instruction, such as "bring me the red block." You type the words and press a key, and the computer does exactly that one thing, nothing more and nothing less.

A command is one line you type into the terminal: the name of a program, then whatever it needs to know, separated by spaces. `python 02_collect_events.py` means "run the program `python`, and use `02_collect_events.py` as the file to run." The terminal reads the line, finds the program, hands it the rest of the words, and waits for it to finish before showing you a new prompt.

A command has the shape `program arg1 arg2 ...`, where each argument is separated by whitespace and quotes group words that contain spaces. Flags like `-r` or `--verbose` are arguments that change behavior rather than naming a file. Running `python 02_collect_events.py --hours 24` calls the `python` interpreter, passes it the script name, and passes the script the flag `--hours` with value `24`; the script itself decides what to do with that flag. The shell exits with a status code, 0 for success and nonzero for failure, which scripts and Makefiles check.

Under the hood, the shell parses the line, expands variables and globs (`*.csv`), then calls `fork` and `exec` to start the named program as a new process, handing it the parsed argument list (`argv`) and the current environment. Standard input, output and error are three file descriptors the shell can redirect (`>`, `<`, `2>`) or connect between commands with a pipe (`|`), which is why `cat data.csv | head` works. Which program actually runs is resolved by searching `PATH` in order for an executable matching the name, so two different `python`s can shadow each other depending on which environment is active. A command fails silently more often than beginners expect, since forgetting to check the exit code, or piping into something that swallows errors, hides a crash you needed to see.

In scripts, `set -euo pipefail` changes the failure behavior: `-e` stops the script on the first nonzero exit, `-u` treats an unset variable as an error, and `pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last one, without which a crashed data-collection step earlier in a pipe can be masked by a successful `head` at the end. Command substitution (`$(...)`) and here-documents let a command's own output feed later commands, which is how Makefiles and CI systems compose pipelines out of otherwise independent programs. A practitioner mistake is treating a command as atomic when it is not: `python 02_collect_events.py` can be interrupted mid-write, leaving a partial file, which is why production pipelines write to a temp path and rename on success. Argument parsing itself is a small design problem, since `argparse` versus a config file versus environment variables trade discoverability against scriptability, and most real pipelines end up using all three.

At scale, a "command" is rarely typed by a person; it is generated by an orchestrator (a workflow scheduler, a CI runner, a Makefile) that must serialize arguments correctly across shells with different quoting rules, which is a persistent source of subtle bugs. Reproducibility work treats the exact command line, environment and working directory as part of the experiment record, not just the code, because two runs of the "same" command with different environment variables can silently produce different numbers. An open practical question is how much of this should move from shell strings to typed, structured command objects, as some workflow engines do, to eliminate an entire class of quoting and escaping bugs.

virtual-environment.def: A private copy of Python and its libraries for one project, so projects do not fight over versions. Create it once, activate it, install into it, and point VS Code and launchd at its Python.
levels: Imagine every toy project gets its own toy box, so the blocks from your spaceship set never get mixed up with the blocks from your castle set. A virtual environment is a toy box just for one project's Python tools.

A virtual environment is a private folder that holds one project's own copy of Python's installed libraries, kept separate from every other project's. You make one with `python -m venv .venv`, turn it on with `source .venv/bin/activate`, and then anything you `pip install` goes into that folder instead of your whole computer. That way, upgrading a library for one project cannot quietly break a different, older project that needed an older version.

Creating an environment (`python -m venv .venv`) copies a small Python interpreter and an empty `site-packages` folder into `.venv`; activating it (`source .venv/bin/activate`) changes your shell's `PATH` so that typing `python` and `pip` finds this copy first. `pip install -r requirements.txt` then installs exactly the pinned versions the project needs, isolated from any other project's environment. Running `which python` after activating should print a path inside `.venv`, and forgetting to activate before installing is the most common way people end up with two conflicting copies of a library.

A venv works by giving each project its own `site-packages` directory and rewriting `sys.path` so the interpreter looks there before the system location; it does not copy the interpreter binary itself, only reference it, which is why the base Python version still matters. This solves the "works on my machine" problem for library versions, but it does not solve interpreter-version drift, differing operating systems, or non-Python system dependencies like a BLAS library, which is why a requirements file is necessary but not sufficient for reproducibility. `conda` environments solve a broader version of the same problem, since they can also pin non-Python binaries, at the cost of a heavier, slower solver. A common failure mode is a stray global `pip install`, run without activating the venv first, that silently pollutes the system Python instead of the project's copy.

Environments are really dependency graphs, and `pip`'s resolver can accept a set of version constraints that is technically satisfiable but numerically different depending on resolution order and what was already cached, which is why plain `requirements.txt` pinning is weaker than a proper lock file (pip-tools, uv, conda-lock) that records every transitive version and hash. On Apple silicon specifically, an environment can silently run under Rosetta instead of natively, producing a working but much slower environment where `platform.machine()` still reports the wrong architecture until you rebuild the interpreter itself as arm64. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming an environment fixes numerical reproducibility: the same pinned versions of numpy or LightGBM can still produce different floating-point results across a different BLAS backend, chip, or thread count. Nested or shadowed environments, such as a venv activated inside a conda environment, or a Jupyter kernel pointed at the wrong interpreter, are a frequent source of "but I installed it" confusion.

At production scale, per-project venvs give way to containers and hermetic build systems (Docker, Nix, Bazel), because reproducibility has to span operating system libraries, drivers and compilers that a venv cannot capture at all. Model registries and experiment trackers increasingly snapshot the resolved environment, a lock file plus a container digest, alongside the model weights, treating the environment as part of the artifact rather than an assumption about the world. An open engineering problem is that hermetic environments are heavier and slower to iterate in than a venv, so most teams live with a tradeoff between the fast, leaky venv workflow for development and a slow, sealed container for anything that has to be reproduced later.

parquet.def: A compressed, column-by-column file format for tables. Small on disk, fast to load, keeps data types. The course stores every cleaned table this way.
levels: Imagine a big box of crayons sorted by color instead of thrown in all mixed up, since it is easier and faster to grab "all the reds" that way. Parquet stores a table sorted like that, by column instead of by row, so the computer can grab just what it needs quickly.

Parquet is a file format for saving tables, like a fancier version of a CSV file. Instead of saving row by row, it saves column by column, and it compresses each column, so the file on disk is much smaller and loads much faster. It also remembers each column's type, that a speed column is a number and a station name is text, so you never have to re-guess it after loading, the way you sometimes do with CSV.

A Parquet file stores each column contiguously and compressed, with metadata describing the schema (column names and types) and statistics per chunk, so a query that only needs `speed` and `station_id` can skip reading every other column entirely. In pandas, `df.to_parquet('data.parquet')` writes it (through the `pyarrow` engine) and `pd.read_parquet('data.parquet')` reads it back with the same dtypes it was saved with, unlike `read_csv`, which has to re-infer types like dates and doesn't preserve categoricals. For a table of 5-minute PeMS rows with many repeated station IDs, Parquet's compression and columnar layout typically make the file five to ten times smaller than the equivalent CSV.

Parquet is a columnar, compressed, self-describing binary format built for analytical workloads: data is organized into row groups, each column within a row group stored contiguously with its own encoding (dictionary encoding for low-cardinality columns like station ID, run-length encoding for repeated values) and per-column min/max statistics that let a reader skip entire row groups without decompressing them. This is why tools like DuckDB can run `SELECT AVG(speed) WHERE station_id = 400001` over a Parquet file far faster than over CSV, without an index, since predicate pushdown uses the statistics to prune, and it only decodes the one column the query touches. Parquet fails to help, and can even hurt, for workloads that need every column of every row, a full table scan with no column pruning, or that mutate data in place, since Parquet files are written once and read many times, not updated incrementally. Choosing a compression codec (snappy for speed, zstd for ratio) and a row-group size are real tuning decisions that trade write time, read time and file size against each other.

The subtlety practitioners get wrong is schema evolution: adding, removing or widening a column across many Parquet files written over time can produce a dataset where different files disagree on schema, and readers that assume a single fixed schema will fail or silently coerce types inconsistently unless the pipeline enforces a schema explicitly. Partitioning a dataset into many small Parquet files by date or station, a common pattern for streaming ingestion, trades query pruning, skipping whole partitions cheaply, against the overhead of opening thousands of small files, and the right partition granularity depends on typical query patterns more than on any general rule. Parquet's compression is also not free at read time, since decompression is real CPU work, so a codec chosen for the smallest file is not always the fastest to read for downstream training. Dictionary encoding, which is a major source of Parquet's advantage on categorical columns like station ID, degrades badly if the column has very high cardinality, at which point it can end up larger than a naive encoding.

At scale, Parquet is the substrate under most data-lake formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi), which layer transactional guarantees, schema versioning and time travel on top of plain Parquet files because Parquet itself has no notion of "this table changed" beyond the files present in a directory. Feature stores for production ML lean on Parquet's columnar pruning to serve wide feature tables efficiently, but they must solve a problem Parquet does not: keeping training-time and serving-time reads of the same features consistent when the underlying files are being rewritten concurrently. An open question in these systems is how to preserve Parquet's read efficiency while getting closer to database-style point updates, which is most of what the newer lakehouse formats are trying to do.

pems.def: Caltrans' Performance Measurement System: the archive of freeway detector readings for California, published as daily text files per district.
levels: Along the freeway there are little sensors buried in the road that count cars as they drive over, like a tiny toll counter that never sleeps. PeMS is the giant filing cabinet where California keeps everything all of those sensors ever counted.

PeMS stands for Performance Measurement System, and it is run by Caltrans, the agency that manages California's highways. Every freeway has detector stations built into the pavement, and every five minutes each one reports how many cars passed, how fast they were going, and how full the lane was. Caltrans publishes all of that as downloadable files, organized by district and by day, and this course's whole project is built on top of them.

PeMS publishes daily text files per Caltrans district, where each row is one detector station's reading for one 5-minute interval: a timestamp, a station ID, flow (vehicle count), occupancy (fraction of time covered), and speed. The Fremont-area stations used in this course sit on District 4 freeways, and a typical day's file for one district has hundreds of thousands of rows across thousands of stations. Detectors go offline or misbehave regularly, since in a district it is normal for a fifth to a third to be unhealthy at any time, so PeMS imputes missing values, and this course treats heavily imputed rows differently from directly measured ones.

PeMS aggregates raw loop-detector and other sensor readings into the standard 5-minute station file, applying quality flags and, for gaps below a certain size, its own imputation before publication; a downstream user has to decide whether to trust that imputation or filter it out, since it is itself a model and not a direct measurement. The data's structure, many stations, each a time series, spatially connected by the freeway network, is why later models in this course move from independent per-row prediction toward architectures (recurrent, then graph-based) that exploit correlation across nearby stations and recent history. PeMS data is public and free, which is unusual for a large-scale sensor dataset and is exactly why it became a standard benchmark source outside of Caltrans' own use. Working with it at any real scale means handling files that don't fit comfortably in memory, inconsistent station metadata across years as stations are added, removed or relocated, and occasional whole-district outages.

PeMS's imputation is worth treating skeptically rather than as ground truth: a station reporting a suspiciously smooth, flat speed for hours is often being filled from a simple model or from neighboring stations, not measured, and folding that into a "true speed" training label without a health flag silently teaches a model to trust fabricated calm periods. Detector health itself drifts with maintenance schedules and can correlate with the outcome you're predicting, such as a detector more likely to fail during a bad storm, which is a subtle source of label leakage or bias if not modeled explicitly. Because PeMS is the shared source for both this project's raw data and public research benchmarks built from PeMS (PEMS-BAY, PeMSD4, PeMSD8), a model that overfits to quirks of a specific era's detector network can look like it's learning traffic dynamics when it is partly learning sensor artifacts. Access patterns matter too, since pulling PeMS at scale means respecting its per-district file structure and rate limits rather than treating it like a queryable database.

At production scale, PeMS-style detector data is one input among several, alongside probe or GPS speeds from vehicles, ramp metering state, and incident feeds, and the interesting systems problem is fusing sparse, unreliable fixed-sensor data with denser but noisier mobile data rather than relying on either alone. PeMS's public benchmarks (PEMS-BAY, METR-LA) are a rare case where production data and academic literature share real lineage, which makes results transferable in both directions, but also means published state-of-the-art numbers can be less impressive on a live deployment where sensor health, coverage and event patterns differ from the curated benchmark subset. An open question for any team building on PeMS is how to keep a production pipeline robust as Caltrans changes detector hardware, coverage or publication format over time, since none of that is contractually guaranteed to stay stable.

occupancy.def: The fraction of the interval the sensor was covered by a vehicle; a stand-in for how densely packed the road is.
levels: Picture a doormat at your front door: occupancy is like counting how much of the time somebody was standing on the mat during the last five minutes. If cars are always sitting on the sensor, the road is packed.

Occupancy is the fraction of a time interval that a vehicle was physically sitting on top of the detector. If a station reports 0.30 occupancy for a five-minute window, that means something was covering the sensor for 30% of those five minutes. It's different from flow, which just counts how many cars passed, since a slow, jammed line of cars can have low flow but high occupancy, because cars are covering the road, just not moving through it quickly.

Occupancy is reported as a fraction (or percent) between 0 and 1, computed by the detector hardware as the total time a vehicle's presence was detected, divided by the interval length. In free-flowing traffic, occupancy is low even with high flow, because cars pass quickly and don't linger over the sensor; as congestion builds, occupancy rises even as flow falls, because cars are closer together and moving slowly or stopped. This inverse relationship, flow drops while occupancy rises, is one of the clearest early signals of a jam, and it's why occupancy is included as a feature alongside speed and flow in this course's models rather than relying on speed alone.

Occupancy is measured directly by the detector as the on-time fraction, not derived from speed or flow, so it carries information those two don't fully capture, especially when speed readings from a struggling detector are noisy or missing. The flow-occupancy relationship traces out the classic fundamental diagram of traffic flow: occupancy near zero with rising flow (free flow), a critical occupancy where flow peaks, and falling flow as occupancy rises further into congestion, the same curve underlying most macroscopic traffic models. Occupancy fails as a clean signal when a detector's calibration drifts, since the "on-time" threshold for detecting a vehicle can shift, or on multi-lane stations where occupancy is aggregated across lanes and can mask one blocked lane against several open ones. Because occupancy and speed carry overlapping but not redundant information, a model like logistic regression benefits from both, and the correlation between them is itself a feature of the traffic regime, not noise to be removed.

Occupancy's dependence on vehicle length is a real subtlety: a fixed loop detector converts an occupancy fraction to a density estimate assuming an average vehicle length, so a lane with many trucks reads a higher occupancy for the same actual vehicle spacing than a lane of only cars, biasing cross-lane and cross-day comparisons if that mix shifts. Occupancy is also more sensitive than speed to a detector's exact physical calibration and to loop-sensitivity settings, which is one reason PeMS's per-station reliability varies more on occupancy than on the coarser flow count. A mistake practitioners make is treating occupancy as a clean, dimensionless quantity comparable across stations, when in practice it needs station-relative normalization, similar to how this course computes speed relative to a station's own free-flow baseline. Because occupancy responds nonlinearly through the fundamental diagram, a small change near the critical point produces a much larger swing in occupancy than the same change in free flow, which makes it a genuinely earlier warning signal for onset of congestion than speed is.

At scale, occupancy from fixed loop detectors is increasingly supplemented or replaced by density estimates from probe vehicle trajectories and connected-vehicle telemetry, which don't require a road-embedded sensor at all and cover far more of the network, though they introduce their own biases from non-uniform vehicle penetration. Research on graph-based traffic models generally treats occupancy, flow and speed as correlated channels of the same underlying state and learns the fundamental-diagram-like relationship implicitly rather than hand-coding it, trading interpretability for flexibility. An open problem at production scale is fusing sparse, well-calibrated occupancy from fixed sensors with denser but less physically grounded probe-derived density in a way that degrades gracefully as either source becomes unreliable.

imputation.def: Filling a missing value with an estimate. PeMS imputes; the course blanks heavily imputed rows and forward-fills short gaps.
levels: If one page of your notebook got a coffee spill and you can't read a word, you might guess it from the sentence before and after. Imputation is guessing a missing number using the numbers around it.

Imputation means filling in a value that's missing from your data with your best guess at what it probably was. If a detector's speed reading is missing for one five-minute slot but the slots right before and after both say 62 miles per hour, a simple imputation just copies that number forward. PeMS does its own imputation before publishing data, and this course adds a second layer: forward-filling short gaps and dropping rows where too much was guessed rather than measured.

A common, simple method is forward-fill (`df.ffill()` or `.fillna(method='ffill')`), which carries the last known value forward to fill a gap, appropriate only for short gaps in a slow-changing quantity like speed. PeMS itself flags rows as imputed, and this course's rule is to forward-fill gaps up to a small number of consecutive missing slots and blank (drop or mark) rows where imputation is heavier than that, rather than trusting an estimate as if it were a real reading. The risk with any imputation is treating a guess as ground truth: a model trained on heavily imputed rows can learn to predict the imputation method's own smoothing behavior instead of real traffic.

Imputation methods range from simple (forward-fill, mean-fill) to model-based (regression on neighboring stations and recent history, k-nearest-neighbors, or a full probabilistic model of the missingness), and the right choice depends on the missingness mechanism: data missing completely at random can be imputed with less bias than data missing because of the very condition you're trying to predict, such as a detector that tends to fail during severe congestion. Naive imputation systematically underestimates variance, since a filled-in value has none of the noise a real measurement would have, which can make a model overconfident if imputed and measured rows are not distinguished. The standard defensive move is to keep an "is imputed" indicator as a feature alongside the filled value, so a downstream model can learn to trust it less. Imputation fails badly when gaps are long or occur at exactly the informative moments, and a detector going dark right as a jam begins is the worst case, since the imputed value likely just repeats the pre-jam pattern.

The rigorous way to think about imputation is as a measurement model: observed value equals true value plus detector noise plus imputation error, where the imputation error is itself the output of another model, often built from neighboring stations and recent history, so any uncertainty estimate that ignores this second source of error is too confident. Multiple imputation, generating several plausible filled datasets and pooling results across them, propagates that uncertainty properly but is rarely used in practice for pipelines at this scale because of the added compute and complexity. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is correlating imputation quality with the label: if detector health itself predicts the outcome, a detector more likely to go dark during a jam, then treating the imputation mask as noise rather than as a feature throws away real signal, and PeMS-scale reality, a fifth to a third of detectors unhealthy at any time in a typical district, makes this a first-order rather than a marginal effect. Downstream, a model that has learned to lean on the smoothness of imputed segments can look artificially accurate offline and then fail in exactly the situations, real, fast-changing congestion, that matter operationally.

At production scale, imputation and detector-health modeling become a system in their own right, a component that estimates per-station reliability continuously and feeds that estimate both into the imputation itself and into every downstream model as a feature, rather than a one-off cleaning step. Modern approaches lean on spatiotemporal models (graph neural networks that treat a station's neighbors and recent history jointly) to impute, which blurs the line between "cleaning the data" and "part of the forecasting model," raising a genuine methodological question about where imputation should stop and prediction should begin. An open research question is how to certify the uncertainty of an imputed value well enough that downstream models and human operators can calibrate their trust in a specific reading, rather than treating all reported values as equally real.

shape.def: The size of each dimension of an array, such as (rows, columns) or (batch, time, channel, station). Most deep-learning bugs are shape bugs.
levels: If you stack blocks into a rectangle, the shape is how many rows tall and how many blocks wide it is. A table of numbers has a shape too: how many rows and how many columns.

The shape of an array tells you its size along each dimension. A table with 1,000 rows and 5 columns has shape `(1000, 5)`; in pandas, `df.shape` gives you exactly that as a pair of numbers. For a deep learning model, arrays can have more dimensions, so a batch of 32 examples, each with 10 time steps and 4 sensor readings, has shape `(32, 10, 4)`, and every layer of the model expects its input to arrive in a particular shape.

`array.shape` returns a tuple, one number per dimension, in order; `numpy` and `pandas` both use this, and PyTorch tensors use `.shape` or `.size()` the same way. A common real shape in this course is `(batch, time, station)` for a window of recent readings across several detector stations feeding a recurrent model, versus `(rows, features)` for the flat table logistic regression and LightGBM expect. Mismatched shapes are the single most common runtime error in model code, since `matmul` fails immediately if the inner dimensions don't agree, so printing `.shape` after each transformation is standard practice for debugging.

Shape mismatches surface at very different points depending on the operation: some (matrix multiplication, concatenation along a fixed axis) fail loudly and immediately, while broadcasting rules in numpy and PyTorch will silently "fix" a shape mismatch by expanding a smaller array, which is convenient when intended and a serious silent bug when not, since a `(100,)` array broadcasting against a `(100, 1)` array instead of raising an error is a classic trap. Reshaping (`.reshape`, `.view`, `.transpose`) changes how the same underlying data is interpreted, and confusing `.reshape` with `.transpose`, since the first reinterprets memory layout and the second actually permutes axes, is a common source of models that train without error but learn nothing useful, because the data reaching each parameter is scrambled relative to what the architecture assumes. For sequence and graph models specifically, getting the batch, time and feature or node axes in the order a layer expects (`batch_first=True` or not, for instance) is exactly the kind of shape detail that has no visible symptom besides poor accuracy until you print shapes at every step.

Shape bugs are insidious specifically because many operations degrade gracefully rather than crashing: broadcasting, implicit type promotion, and squeeze or unsqueeze mismatches can all produce a tensor of a plausible-looking shape that is nonetheless semantically wrong, so a model can train, converge, and even report a reasonable loss while learning from corrupted or misaligned data. A related subtlety is that shape correctness is necessary but not sufficient: two tensors can have identical shape while their axes carry different meaning, such as station-major versus time-major ordering, which no shape check catches and which only a semantic assertion or a unit test on known input can catch. Practitioners commonly under-invest in shape assertions (`assert x.shape == (batch, T, S)`) at module boundaries, treating them as clutter, right up until a refactor silently swaps two axes and a week of training runs on scrambled data before anyone notices. In graph and spatiotemporal models specifically, the number of axes that matter grows (batch, time, node, channel, and sometimes edge), and the einsum-style explicit notation (`'btnc,cd->btnd'`) is often worth the verbosity precisely because it makes every axis's role unambiguous.

At production scale, shape contracts between components, a data pipeline, a feature store, a model, a serving layer, are often enforced with typed schemas and shape-checked interfaces (via tools like `jaxtyping`, `torchtyping`, or protocol buffers with fixed dimensions) precisely because a silent shape or axis-order mismatch between two independently deployed services is one of the more common causes of an ML incident that produces plausible-looking but wrong outputs rather than a visible crash. Dynamic and variable shapes, such as a variable number of active stations on a graph or ragged sequence lengths, push teams toward padding-and-masking schemes or sparse tensor formats, each with real performance tradeoffs on accelerator hardware that favor fixed, regular shapes. An open engineering problem is verifying shape and semantic axis-order correctness automatically across a pipeline of independently versioned components, rather than relying on runtime asserts that only catch a mismatch after it has already reached production.

rolling.def: A window of the last n rows; `.mean()`, `.std()`, `.sum()`, `.max()` summarize it. Rows must be in time order first.
levels: Imagine you only ever look at your last three days of homework grades and average them, and every new day you drop the oldest one and add the newest. That sliding little window of "the last few" is what rolling means.

`rolling(n)` in pandas creates a window that always covers the most recent n rows, and slides forward one row at a time as you move down the table. Calling `.mean()` on it gives you the average of the last n rows at every point, `.std()` gives the spread, and `.max()` gives the largest value. It only makes sense if your rows are already sorted in time order, since a rolling average of scrambled rows is meaningless.

`df['speed'].rolling(6).mean()` computes, for each row, the average of that row and the 5 rows before it, six 5-minute slots, or 30 minutes, in this course's data. By default the window is right-aligned, meaning it only looks backward, which matters because a feature that peeks at future rows can't be used at prediction time; `rolling(6, center=True)` would look ahead and must never be used for a feature. `min_periods` controls how many rows are required before a window produces a value at all, so with `min_periods=1`, the first few rows compute an average over fewer than 6 rows instead of returning missing values.

Rolling windows can be defined by row count (`rolling(6)`) or by a fixed time offset (`rolling('30min')`), which differ meaningfully when rows are not perfectly evenly spaced, since a row-count window silently assumes uniform spacing, while a time-offset window is robust to a missing or duplicated row. `rolling` composes with `groupby`, so `df.groupby('station_id')['speed'].rolling(6).mean()` computes a separate rolling average per station without them leaking into each other, which is essential in this course since a citywide rolling average across mixed stations would be meaningless. Rolling features are the mechanism behind lag- and trend-based features, such as a 30-minute rolling mean of speed or a rolling standard deviation of occupancy as a volatility signal, and they fail specifically at the start of every group's time series, where `min_periods` and NaN-handling decisions directly affect how many usable rows a station contributes. A subtlety is that `rolling` operates on whatever order the DataFrame is currently in, not on a datetime index automatically, so an unsorted or re-indexed table silently produces a wrong rolling calculation with no error.

The choice between count-based and time-based rolling windows interacts with how you handle irregular sampling and detector dropouts: a count-based window over a station with several missing 5-minute slots quietly spans a longer wall-clock interval than intended, biasing a "last 30 minutes" feature toward being a "last 40 minutes" feature without any signal that this happened, whereas a time-based window handles the gap correctly but can include fewer real observations than expected. Rolling statistics are also autocorrelated by construction, since adjacent rows share most of the same underlying observations, which inflates apparent smoothness and is a common reason cross-validation on rolling-derived features overstates performance unless folds respect time order, rolling-origin evaluation, not random shuffling. Practitioners often forget that a rolling window computed before a train/test split can leak future information across the boundary if the split isn't strictly time-based, since a window near the split point reaches slightly into the other side. Choice of statistic matters too: `rolling().std()` on a short window is a noisy estimate with few degrees of freedom, and using it as a feature without accounting for that noise can make a model overreact to windows that happened to be short due to missing data.

At production scale, rolling features computed offline in pandas must be reproduced exactly at serving time from a streaming feed, which is a genuine engineering challenge, since a streaming rolling window has to handle late-arriving or out-of-order detector rows, decide how long to wait before finalizing a window's value, and guarantee the online computation matches the offline training computation bit-for-bit or close to it, or the model sees systematically different features live than it did in training. Feature stores generally solve this with a shared definition, the window logic specified once and compiled to both a batch job and a streaming operator, specifically to eliminate training-serving skew in exactly this class of feature. An open problem at scale is bounding staleness guarantees for rolling features under real network and sensor failure patterns, since a rolling window's value is only as trustworthy as the assumption that its constituent rows arrived roughly on time.

seed.def: A fixed starting point for random numbers, so a run can be repeated exactly.
levels: When you shuffle a deck of cards, if you start the same special way every time, you get the same shuffle every time. A seed is that special starting point for a computer's "random" numbers, so the shuffle can be repeated exactly.

Computers don't generate truly random numbers; they use a formula that produces numbers that look random, starting from a starting value called a seed. If you set `random_state=0` or use `numpy.random.default_rng(0)`, you get the exact same sequence of "random" numbers every time you run the code. This matters because it lets you rerun an experiment, splitting the same data the same way or shuffling rows the same way, and get identical results to compare against.

In scikit-learn, passing `random_state=0` to something like `train_test_split` or a model fixes every random choice it makes internally, so re-running the same code produces the same split or the same trained weights. In numpy's newer API, `rng = numpy.random.default_rng(0)` creates a dedicated random number generator object seeded at 0, and calls like `rng.choice(...)` draw from it, which is preferred over the older global `numpy.random.seed(0)` because it doesn't affect unrelated code that also uses randomness. For example, `df.sample(1, random_state=0)` always draws the exact same row, which is useful for writing a repeatable spot-check.

A seed initializes a pseudo-random number generator's internal state, and everything the generator produces afterward is a deterministic function of that state, random only in the sense of passing statistical tests for randomness, not in being unpredictable if you know the seed and algorithm. Reproducibility with a seed requires controlling every source of randomness in a pipeline, not just one: numpy, Python's own `random` module, a model library's internal generator, and, for anything on a GPU, a separate CUDA-level random state and sometimes non-determinism from parallel reduction order that a seed alone cannot fix. Different generator algorithms (numpy's legacy `RandomState` versus the newer `Generator` from `default_rng`) can produce different sequences from the same seed number, so "seed 0" is not portable across libraries or even across numpy versions without care. Seeding does not make an experiment's conclusion more valid, only its individual run more reproducible, which is why a single seeded run can still be an unrepresentative draw, and serious evaluation reports results across multiple seeds rather than one.

The distinction between reproducibility and robustness is where practitioners most often go wrong: a model's headline metric under one fixed seed can look stable while actually depending heavily on which seed you happened to pick, so any comparison between two models or configurations should really report variance across several seeds, not a single seeded run that could favor one side by chance. Seeding a train/test split additionally interacts with time-ordered data in a way that plain seeded shuffling gets wrong, since a fixed seed guarantees the same random split, but a random split is the wrong split entirely for a time series problem like this course's, where evaluation should be rolling-origin, not randomly shuffled, no matter how carefully seeded. On parallel and GPU hardware, true bit-for-bit determinism from a seed often requires disabling certain fast, non-deterministic parallel algorithms, which is a real accuracy-versus-speed-versus-reproducibility tradeoff that teams have to decide on deliberately. A subtler mistake is seeding once at the top of a long pipeline and assuming every downstream random draw is now controlled, when a library update, a new randomness source, or code reordering silently changes what each seeded call actually produces.

At production and research scale, exact reproducibility from a seed becomes probabilistic rather than guaranteed, because distributed training introduces non-determinism from asynchronous gradient aggregation, floating-point summation order, and hardware-specific kernel implementations that a software-level seed does not control. Research organizations increasingly report results as a distribution over seeds, mean and spread across five or ten runs, precisely because single-seed comparisons have contributed to false claims of improvement in the literature, since an effect smaller than seed-to-seed variance is not a real effect. An open infrastructure problem is that full bit-for-bit reproducibility and maximum hardware throughput are often in tension, so teams have to explicitly choose, run by run, whether they need one or the other.

prevalence.def: The share of rows that are positive. Small here, which is why accuracy is useless and average precision is used.
levels: If you have a big jar of one hundred jellybeans and only three are the yucky flavor, prevalence is how many out of the hundred are yucky. In this course, "slow traffic" rows are the rare, yucky-flavor ones.

Prevalence is the fraction of all your data rows that are the thing you're trying to predict, the positive class. If out of 100,000 rows only 3,000 are labeled "slow traffic," the prevalence is 3%. Low prevalence matters a lot for how you judge a model: a model that always guesses "not slow" would already be right 97% of the time, so plain accuracy is a bad way to tell whether it's actually useful.

Prevalence is computed as (number of positive rows) / (total rows); in this course it's a few percent, since slow-traffic events are rare relative to all 5-minute station readings. Because prevalence is low, accuracy is a misleading metric, since always predicting the majority class scores high accuracy while being useless, so the course uses average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve, instead, since it directly measures how well the model ranks true positives near the top. Prevalence also isn't fixed: `df['label'].mean()` computed separately by season or by time of day can shift noticeably, since slow traffic is more common at rush hour and during storms.

Low prevalence changes which metrics are informative and which are not: ROC-AUC can look deceptively good under class imbalance because it's dominated by the much larger number of true negatives, while average precision, the area under precision-recall, focuses on how well the model ranks the rare positives, which matches the actual operational question of whether the top of the ranked list is mostly real slow-traffic events. Prevalence also determines the achievable precision at any given recall, since a rarer positive class makes high precision fundamentally harder to reach at the same recall, independent of model quality, so precision-recall curves for problems with different prevalence are not directly comparable without normalizing for that. A model trained naively on low-prevalence data can also learn a poorly calibrated probability output, since the raw score from a tree ensemble in particular tends to be biased toward the majority class, which is a separate problem from ranking quality and is why this course treats calibration, via isotonic regression, as a distinct step from choosing a threshold. Techniques like class weighting or resampling address training-time imbalance but change what the model's raw probability output means, so they interact with calibration and threshold choice rather than being free fixes.

Prevalence is not a fixed property of the problem but a property of the sampling window, and treating it as constant is a common mistake: seasonal effects, roadwork and weather shift the true rate of slow-traffic events, so a model calibrated and thresholded on one period's prevalence will systematically over- or under-alarm when deployed into a period with different prevalence, even if the model's discrimination ability, its ranking quality, hasn't degraded at all. This is why monitoring prevalence itself, alongside metric values, is part of a serious deployment, since a drop in average precision could mean the model got worse, or it could mean prevalence dropped and the ranking task got intrinsically harder, and those call for different responses. A related subtlety is that average precision itself is sensitive to prevalence in a way practitioners sometimes forget when comparing across time windows or across stations with very different base rates, and a fair comparison sometimes requires reporting metrics conditional on prevalence, or using a prevalence-independent measure of ranking quality. Threshold choice downstream of prevalence is itself a decision under a cost model, not a statistical fact, since the "right" threshold moves as the cost of a false alarm versus a missed jam changes, and that tradeoff is a business decision the model's raw output does not make for you.

At production scale, prevalence drift is one of the most common causes of a model quietly going stale without an obvious code or data bug, since a real change in the world, a new highway interchange opening or a shift in commute patterns, changes the base rate the model was calibrated against, and monitoring systems have to distinguish that from actual model degradation using metrics like the population stability index alongside recomputed average precision. Extremely low-prevalence problems more broadly (fraud, rare medical events, safety-critical anomalies) push practitioners toward specialized techniques, anomaly-detection framings, extreme value theory, or active learning to enrich rare positive examples, when the positive rate becomes too small for standard supervised metrics to be statistically stable over a practical evaluation window. An open question in these systems is how to set alerting thresholds that remain well-calibrated automatically as prevalence drifts, rather than requiring a human to notice and manually recalibrate.

precision.def: Precision is the share of alarms that were right; recall is the share of real jams that were alarmed. Raising one usually lowers the other.
levels: If you have a smoke alarm, precision is how often it goes off only when there's really a fire, and recall is how many real fires it actually catches. A jumpy alarm that goes off for burnt toast has bad precision; a lazy alarm that misses real fires has bad recall.

Precision answers "of the times the model said 'slow traffic,' how often was it right?" Recall answers "of all the times traffic really was slow, how many did the model catch?" If the model raises 100 alarms and 80 were real jams, precision is 80%; if there were 200 real jams total and it caught those 80, recall is 40%. You usually can't max out both at once, since being pickier about alarms, raising precision, tends to mean you miss more real jams, lowering recall.

Precision = true positives / (true positives + false positives); recall = true positives / (true positives + false negatives). Both come from the same confusion matrix, and moving the decision threshold on the model's score trades one against the other: a lower threshold catches more real jams (higher recall) but raises more false alarms (lower precision), and a higher threshold does the reverse. A precision-recall curve plots this tradeoff across every possible threshold, and the area under it, average precision, summarizes overall ranking quality independent of any one threshold choice.

Precision and recall are computed from a binary decision at a chosen threshold on the model's continuous score, so they describe an operating point, not the model itself, since the same model can be reported at very different precision-recall pairs depending purely on where the threshold is set, which is why comparing two models' precision at arbitrary, unmatched thresholds is not meaningful. The F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, collapses the tradeoff to one number under an implicit assumption that false positives and false negatives cost the same, which is rarely true operationally, since for a traffic alert system, missing a real jam and crying wolf plausibly have very different real-world costs, so F1 is often the wrong single number to optimize. Precision and recall both depend on prevalence: at very low prevalence, achieving high precision is intrinsically harder even for a strong model, since a small false-positive rate among a huge number of negatives still produces many false alarms in absolute terms. They fail as useful metrics on their own when reported at a single, unstated threshold, since a reader can't tell whether a reported precision reflects a genuinely better model or simply a more conservative threshold.

The precision-recall curve's shape, not just the area under it, carries information a single average-precision number discards, since a curve that holds high precision until very high recall and then collapses sharply behaves very differently in deployment than one that degrades gradually, even at matched average precision, and the right operating threshold depends on which shape you have. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is optimizing average precision in development and then choosing a deployment threshold based on a different, later criterion, say a fixed alert budget per day, without re-checking that the model's precision-recall behavior near that specific operating point is actually good, since average precision integrates over the whole curve and can look fine while the one region you actually operate in is weak. Precision and recall computed on a held-out test set are themselves estimates with sampling variance, particularly at low prevalence where the number of positive examples in any given test window can be small, so a single-window precision-recall comparison between models can be noise rather than signal without confidence intervals or multiple evaluation windows. In a real alerting system, precision and recall interact with the cost structure asymmetrically over time, since a run of false alarms erodes operator trust in a way that a matched number of one-off missed alarms might not, which is a dynamic that the static metrics don't capture at all.

At production scale, precision and recall are tracked as continuously monitored, prevalence-adjusted metrics rather than one-off evaluation numbers, since deployment prevalence drifts and a model's precision at a fixed threshold moves with it even when the model itself hasn't changed or degraded. Multi-stakeholder systems often need multiple simultaneous operating points, such as a high-precision threshold for an automated action and a high-recall threshold for flagging items to a human reviewer, which means precision and recall have to be reported and monitored as a family of thresholds, not a single pair. An open research question in imbalanced, high-stakes settings is how to design objective functions and evaluation protocols that better reflect asymmetric real-world costs than precision, recall or their averages do on their own, since none of the standard metrics are actually the loss function decision-makers care about.

population-stability-index.def: One number comparing a feature's distribution now with training. Below 0.1 stable, above 0.25 moved.
levels: Imagine you counted your friends' favorite ice cream flavors on the first day of school, and you count again in the winter to see if everyone changed their mind. PSI is one number that says how much the count changed.

The population stability index, or PSI, compares a feature's distribution today against its distribution back when the model was trained, and gives you a single number summarizing how different they are. It works by splitting the feature into bins, say, ranges of speed, checking what fraction of rows fell into each bin during training versus what fraction falls into each bin now, and combining the differences. A small PSI, below about 0.1, means the feature looks about the same as before; a PSI above about 0.25 means it has shifted enough to worry about.

PSI is computed as the sum, over bins, of (current % − training %) × ln(current % / training %), where the feature is bucketed into the same fixed bins both times, typically deciles from the training distribution. In this course, PSI is computed per feature, average speed, occupancy, hour of day, comparing the last week's values against the training window, as part of routine monitoring. A rule of thumb treats PSI < 0.1 as stable, 0.1–0.25 as a moderate shift worth watching, and > 0.25 as a real distribution change that likely means the model's assumptions no longer hold.

PSI is a discretized, symmetrized measure related to the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two distributions binned the same way; unlike a raw statistical distance, it's designed to be interpretable at fixed thresholds (0.1, 0.25) that practitioners have converged on as rough conventions rather than anything derived from theory. It's computed per feature independently, which means it can miss a shift that only shows up jointly, such as two features whose individual marginal distributions look stable while their correlation has changed entirely, a real limitation for a spatially and temporally correlated problem like traffic. PSI also depends heavily on the binning choice: too few bins hides a real shift, too many makes the statistic noisy on any bin with few observations, and it's undefined, or requires a small-count adjustment, if a bin that had training-time mass has exactly zero current observations. It fails specifically for features with heavy-tailed or highly seasonal distributions, like traffic speed at different hours, where a "shift" it flags might just be the ordinary daily cycle rather than genuine drift, unless it's computed conditional on time of day.

PSI is a useful triage signal, not a diagnosis: a high PSI tells you a feature's distribution moved, but not whether that movement matters for the model's actual predictions, since a feature can drift substantially in a region the model barely relies on, or drift only slightly in exactly the region that drives its decisions, which is why serious monitoring pairs PSI with a direct check of prediction or performance drift, not PSI alone. A mistake practitioners make is computing PSI against a fixed, aging training-time reference forever, when a rolling or periodically refreshed reference window is usually more appropriate for a naturally seasonal quantity like traffic, or every winter will trip every summer-trained threshold. PSI's additive, per-bin structure also means a large positive shift in one bin can be partly canceled by a large negative shift in another when they're of similar magnitude but different sign contribution, though this is less of an issue than with a naive difference-of-means statistic because PSI sums absolute-value-like contributions, not signed ones. Choosing PSI over other divergence measures, population-level KL, Jensen-Shannon, or a two-sample statistical test like Kolmogorov-Smirnov, is mostly a practical decision, since PSI is cheap, well-understood by non-statisticians on a team, and has established thresholds, rather than a claim that it's the most statistically powerful choice.

At production scale, PSI, or a family of PSI-like statistics, one per feature, is usually just the front layer of a larger drift-detection system that also monitors label distribution, prediction distribution, and joint feature correlations, since per-feature marginal drift alone catches only a subset of the ways a deployed model's world can change under it. Automated systems increasingly try to move beyond fixed thresholds (0.1, 0.25) toward statistically calibrated alerting that accounts for the natural sampling variance of PSI at a given window size and feature cardinality, since a rigid threshold either fires too often on noise at small sample sizes or too rarely to be useful at very large ones. An open problem is closing the loop from a PSI alert to an actual decision automatically, since flagging drift is comparatively easy, but deciding whether to retrain, roll back, or simply widen a confidence interval in response is still mostly a human judgment call layered on top of the statistic.

gradient.def: The direction in which the loss rises fastest, one number per parameter. Training steps against it.
levels: Imagine you're standing on a hill in the fog and can't see anything, but you can feel which way is steepest under your feet. The gradient is that feeling, which way is uphill, so you can step the opposite way to get down.

The gradient tells a model which direction to change each of its numbers (its parameters, or weights) to make its mistakes bigger, so training moves the opposite way to make mistakes smaller. It's really one number per parameter, so for a model with a thousand weights, the gradient is a thousand numbers, each saying "increase this one" or "decrease this one" and by how much. Gradient descent just means: compute the gradient, take a small step against it, and repeat, over and over, until the mistakes stop shrinking much.

For logistic regression's cross-entropy loss, the gradient with respect to a weight w works out to a strikingly simple formula: ∂loss/∂w = (p − y)·x, where p is the model's predicted probability, y is the true label (0 or 1), and x is the input value; the gradient with respect to the bias is just (p − y). Training uses the update rule w ← w − η∇L, where η (eta) is the learning rate, a small step size, and ∇L is the gradient; too large a step and training diverges, too small and it crawls. Because the sigmoid's own derivative is p(1 − p), and the chain rule cancels that term against the derivative of the log-loss, the gradient simplifies down to nothing more than "error times input," which is why logistic regression trains so cleanly.

The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to every parameter, and it points in the direction of steepest ascent of the loss surface, so gradient descent moves against it. For a convex loss like logistic regression's, following the gradient with a small enough, well-chosen learning rate is guaranteed to converge to the global minimum; for a non-convex loss, as in any neural network, the gradient only guarantees convergence to some local stationary point, not the global optimum, and the path taken depends on initialization. Computing gradients for a model with many layers is done by backpropagation, which is really the chain rule applied mechanically layer by layer, propagating the error backward from the output. Gradients fail, vanish toward zero or explode toward infinity, in deep or recurrent networks when many small or large derivatives multiply together across layers, which is a central practical obstacle that architectures like GRUs and techniques like gradient clipping and careful initialization exist specifically to address.

Stochastic gradient descent computes the gradient from a random mini-batch rather than the full dataset, which makes each step a noisy but unbiased estimate of the true gradient, and that noise is not purely a nuisance, since it helps the optimizer escape shallow local minima and saddle points in non-convex losses, so tuning batch size is partly about tuning how much of that beneficial noise you want. Momentum-based optimizers, Adam in particular, track a running estimate of the gradient's first and second moments rather than using the raw gradient directly, which practitioners often use as a black box without understanding that this changes the effective step size adaptively per parameter, sometimes in ways that interact badly with weight decay if implemented naively, which is the reason decoupled weight decay, as in AdamW, was introduced. A subtlety many miss is that a near-zero gradient does not mean "optimal," since it equally describes a saddle point, of which high-dimensional non-convex losses have vastly more than true local minima, so gradient magnitude alone is a weak stopping signal. Gradient-based optimization also assumes the loss is differentiable almost everywhere, which fails at points like a ReLU's kink, handled in practice with a subgradient convention that works well empirically despite not being fully justified by classical convex theory.

At the scale of large models, computing and communicating gradients efficiently across many accelerators is itself a major systems problem, since gradient synchronization, compression, and mixed-precision arithmetic all trade numerical fidelity against speed, and a poorly chosen precision can silently corrupt small gradients toward zero, stalling learning without an obvious error. Differentiable programming extends the gradient idea past standard neural networks to differentiating through simulators, optimization layers, and physical models, which is an active research direction relevant to any project that would like to fit a physics-based traffic model's parameters directly against real detector data using gradients. An open question at scale is how to get useful, well-behaved gradient signal through long computational chains, deep networks, long rollouts, discrete decisions, without it vanishing, exploding, or becoming so noisy that it stops being informative at all.

gradient-boosting.def: Hundreds of small trees, each fitted to the errors of the ones before; their sum is the score. LightGBM is the fast library used in production here.
levels: Imagine a team of students each fixing a small mistake left by the student before them, one after another, until the answer is really good. Gradient boosting builds a model that way, out of lots of small trees, each one cleaning up what the last one got wrong.

Gradient boosting builds a model out of many small decision trees, one after another, where each new tree is trained specifically to fix the errors the trees before it are still making. Instead of one big tree trying to get everything right, you get hundreds of small, weak trees whose combined guesses add up to a strong one. LightGBM is a fast, popular software library for training this kind of model, and it's the one this course uses for its main production model, since it trains quickly even on large tables like PeMS data.

A gradient boosting model's prediction is the sum of many trees' outputs: score = tree1(x) + tree2(x) + ... + treeN(x), where each tree after the first is fit to the negative gradient of the loss, roughly, the errors the model so far is making. Key LightGBM settings include `num_leaves` (how complex each tree can be), `learning_rate` (how much each tree's contribution counts), and `min_data_in_leaf` (a guard against trees overfitting to tiny groups of rows); LightGBM also handles categorical features like station ID natively, without needing one-hot encoding. Training in code looks like `lgb.LGBMClassifier(num_leaves=31, learning_rate=0.05).fit(X_train, y_train)`, and it typically beats logistic regression on this course's traffic data because it can capture nonlinear interactions between features like hour-of-day and occupancy automatically.

Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space (Friedman, 2001): instead of updating parameters against a gradient, each step adds a new function, a small tree, chosen to approximately follow the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions, evaluated at every training point. LightGBM specifically uses histogram-based split finding (bucketing continuous features to speed up choosing the best split) and leaf-wise tree growth (always splitting the leaf with the largest loss reduction, rather than growing level by level), which makes it faster than earlier implementations like classic gradient boosting or even XGBoost's default settings, at the cost of leaf-wise trees being more prone to overfitting on small datasets if `num_leaves` isn't controlled. Gradient boosting handles nonlinearity and feature interactions without manual feature engineering, unlike logistic regression, but it can overfit badly with too many trees or too little regularization, and it doesn't extrapolate sensibly outside the range of training data, since each tree's prediction is a step function that's flat beyond the range it saw. It also has no inherent notion of time or sequence, since every row is treated as independent, so temporal structure like lag features has to be engineered explicitly rather than learned by the architecture.

LightGBM's leaf-wise growth strategy is a genuine tradeoff practitioners often don't fully internalize: it can find lower training loss faster than level-wise growth for a fixed number of leaves, but it also produces deeper, more asymmetric trees that overfit more readily, which is why `num_leaves`, `max_depth` and `min_data_in_leaf` need to be tuned together rather than any one in isolation, since a large `num_leaves` with a shallow `max_depth` cap behaves very differently than the same `num_leaves` unconstrained. The second-order approximation LightGBM and XGBoost both use, fitting each tree using both the gradient and the Hessian (curvature) of the loss, not just the gradient, gives more accurate per-leaf updates than plain gradient boosting, especially for loss functions like cross-entropy where the curvature varies a lot across the score range. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating raw tree-ensemble scores as calibrated probabilities: they're optimized to separate classes well, to rank correctly, not to be numerically accurate probabilities, which is why this course adds a separate calibration step, isotonic regression, rather than using the raw LightGBM output directly for probability-sensitive decisions. Early stopping on a validation set, categorical feature handling via LightGBM's built-in support rather than one-hot encoding, and careful choice of the evaluation metric during training, which need not match the deployment metric, are all decisions that materially change results but are easy to leave at defaults without realizing the cost.

At production scale, gradient boosted trees remain a workhorse for tabular data specifically because they're fast to train, fast to serve, robust to unscaled and mixed-type features, and competitive with or better than deep learning on many structured prediction tasks, a pattern that has held up surprisingly consistently across the tabular-deep-learning literature. Serving them at low latency at scale involves compiling the trained ensemble into optimized native code or specialized formats rather than calling the training library directly, since inference latency for hundreds of trees times millions of requests is a real cost. An open research question, revisited regularly, is why gradient boosted trees continue to outperform deep learning on most tabular benchmarks despite deep learning's dominance elsewhere, with current explanations centering on trees' natural fit to non-smooth, heterogeneous, low-sample-size tabular structure that gradient-based neural training handles less naturally.

recurrent-network.def: A model that reads a sequence step by step, keeping a hidden state; the GRU uses gates to decide what to remember.
levels: Imagine reading a story one word at a time, and after every word you update a little note to yourself about what's happened so far, so you don't have to remember every single word. A recurrent network reads data the same way, one step at a time, keeping a running note called its hidden state.

A recurrent network reads a sequence, like a station's speed readings over the last hour, one 5-minute reading at a time, and after each step it updates an internal "memory," called the hidden state, that summarizes everything it's seen so far. A GRU (gated recurrent unit) is a specific, popular kind of recurrent network that has small gates deciding how much of the old memory to keep and how much of the new information to let in. This lets it handle sequences where recent events usually matter more, but something from a while ago can still matter too.

A basic recurrent network updates its hidden state at each time step as a function of the current input and the previous hidden state: ht = f(Wx·xt + Wh·ht-1 + b), and its final hidden state, or its state at each step, can be fed to an output layer to make a prediction. A plain recurrent network struggles to remember information from many steps back, because the same weight matrix is applied repeatedly and gradients tend to vanish over long sequences; a GRU fixes this with an update gate and a reset gate, learned functions that control how much of the previous state to keep versus overwrite at each step. In code, PyTorch's `nn.GRU(input_size, hidden_size)` takes a sequence of shape `(batch, time, features)` and returns a hidden state sequence you can use to predict, for example, whether a station will be slow 30 minutes from now.

Understanding ARIMA-style time series models first clarifies why lag features work in the simpler logistic regression and LightGBM models in this course, and what a recurrent network adds beyond them: nonlinearity in how past values combine, the ability to take exogenous inputs, like occupancy and flow alongside speed, naturally within the same sequence, and parameters shared across every time step and, if trained that way, across every station, rather than a fixed, hand-chosen set of lag features. A GRU's gates are themselves small learned neural network layers, a sigmoid over a linear combination of the current input and previous hidden state, which is why a GRU has more parameters and requires more data to train well than a plain recurrent unit, but converges more reliably because the gating mitigates the vanishing gradient problem that plain RNNs suffer over long sequences. Recurrent networks fail, or need care, when sequences are very long, since gates alone don't fully solve vanishing gradients at hundreds or thousands of steps, which is part of why attention-based architectures largely replaced RNNs for very long sequences, when data is irregularly sampled, since recurrent networks implicitly assume a fixed step size, or when there's too little training data relative to the model's parameter count, which favors the simpler logistic regression or LightGBM baselines in this course instead. Training is done via backpropagation through time, unrolling the recurrence across all time steps and applying the chain rule backward through the whole unrolled graph, which is more expensive and more prone to instability than training a non-sequential model.

The GRU versus LSTM choice is a real but often overstated tradeoff in practice: GRUs have fewer parameters, since they merge the LSTM's separate forget and input gates and drop its distinct cell state, train slightly faster, and empirically perform comparably to LSTMs on most tasks, so the choice is usually more about engineering convenience than a principled difference in modeling power for a given problem. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming a recurrent network will automatically discover the right lag structure without help, since in practice feeding it well-chosen engineered features, rolling means, lags, alongside raw values often still improves performance over raw sequences alone, because gradient-based training doesn't always find every useful nonlinear combination on its own within a practical training budget. Recurrent architectures for spatiotemporal data like PeMS also face a genuine architectural choice about how to handle multiple correlated stations: running one shared GRU per station independently ignores spatial correlation entirely, while naively concatenating all stations into one input vector treats the network's fixed topology as arbitrary feature order, which is exactly the gap that graph-based architectures (DCRNN, STGCN, Graph WaveNet) exist to fill by combining a recurrent or convolutional temporal component with an explicit graph structure over stations. Vanishing and exploding gradients, gradient clipping, and the choice of sequence length to backpropagate through, truncated versus full backpropagation through time, remain real, hands-on tuning decisions rather than settled defaults, especially as sequence length grows.

At production scale, plain recurrent networks including GRUs have been substantially displaced in much of the sequence-modeling literature by attention-based and transformer architectures, which parallelize across the sequence dimension far better on modern accelerator hardware and handle long-range dependencies more directly, though GRUs remain attractive in latency- and memory-constrained settings, on-device or low-power inference, precisely because their step-by-step, constant-memory computation is cheap compared to attention's full-sequence cost. For spatiotemporal traffic forecasting specifically, the state of the art has moved toward graph neural networks that combine a recurrent or convolutional temporal component with learned or physical graph structure over the road network (Graph WaveNet, DCRNN, and their successors), treating a plain per-station GRU as a reasonable, well-understood baseline rather than a frontier method. An open research question is how to combine the efficiency and simplicity of gated recurrence with the long-range and multi-entity reasoning that attention and graph structure provide, without paying the full computational cost of either at inference time.

isotonic-regression.def: A step function that only goes up, fitted to map raw scores to observed frequencies. The calibration method used.
levels: Imagine you sort your test scores from lowest to highest and draw a staircase that only ever goes up, never down, to match how often you actually got things right. Isotonic regression is a computer doing exactly that staircase-fitting trick.

Tree-based models like LightGBM produce scores that rank things correctly, since higher score really does mean more likely, but the actual numbers aren't trustworthy as real probabilities. Isotonic regression fixes this: it fits a step function, one that's only allowed to go up (or stay flat) as the raw score increases, so that within each step the model's stated probability actually matches how often things were true in that group. It's the calibration method this course uses to turn a raw LightGBM score into a number you can genuinely read as "this is a 73% chance of slow traffic."

Isotonic regression fits a non-decreasing step function g(score) → probability by minimizing squared error subject to the constraint that the function never decreases as the raw score increases; in scikit-learn this is `IsotonicRegression().fit(raw_scores, true_labels)` on a held-out calibration set, separate from the data used to train the original model. The result is applied after the model: `calibrated_prob = iso.predict(model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])`. A reliability diagram, predicted probability on one axis, observed frequency on the other, shows the fix directly: before calibration the points often sit off the diagonal, and after fitting isotonic regression, they should sit close to it.

Isotonic regression solves a constrained least-squares problem (via the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm) to find the best-fitting monotonic step function mapping raw scores to calibrated probabilities, and because it makes no assumption about the shape of the miscalibration beyond monotonicity, it can fix arbitrarily shaped calibration curves that a simpler parametric method like Platt scaling, which fits a sigmoid, cannot. This flexibility is also its weakness: with limited calibration data, isotonic regression can overfit, producing a jagged step function that memorizes noise in the calibration set rather than a smooth true relationship, which is why Platt scaling is often preferred with small calibration sets and isotonic regression with larger ones. Calibration must be fit on data the original model never trained on, since using the training set itself for calibration would just reproduce the model's own overconfidence rather than correct it, so this course reserves a separate calibration split distinct from both the training and final test data. Isotonic regression only reorders and remaps scores monotonically; it cannot fix a model whose ranking is wrong to begin with, since a monotonic transformation preserves rank order exactly, so calibration is strictly a probability-accuracy fix, not a discrimination-quality fix.

A subtlety practitioners routinely miss is that calibration is dataset- and time-window-specific: a calibration map fit on one period's data assumes the relationship between raw score and true frequency is stable, and under prevalence drift, which this course expects, given seasonal traffic patterns, that assumption breaks, so a calibration map needs periodic refitting, not a one-time fix. Isotonic regression's flexibility becomes a real liability with small calibration sets or with scores that have many ties, common with tree ensembles, which produce a limited number of distinct leaf-combination scores, since the fitted step function can end up with very wide, coarse steps that lose most of the score's resolution; some practitioners smooth or bin the isotonic fit as a compromise. The choice of calibration metric to evaluate afterward matters too, since expected calibration error, binned average gap between predicted and observed frequency, and the Brier score capture different aspects of calibration quality, and a model can look well-calibrated on one while being poorly calibrated on the other, particularly in the sparse, low-prevalence tail this course's slow-traffic problem lives in. Calibration is also not free with respect to ranking-sensitive metrics: isotonic regression preserves rank exactly by construction, so it never changes average precision, but downstream systems that threshold on the calibrated probability rather than the raw score are implicitly relying on both the ranking and the calibration being good simultaneously.

At production scale, calibration has to be monitored and refreshed continuously rather than fit once, since prevalence and score distributions drift, and a stale calibration map can silently make a model's probabilities misleading even while its underlying ranking quality, average precision, stays perfectly fine, which is exactly the kind of failure that a metric dashboard tracking only ranking metrics would miss entirely. Multi-model and multi-population systems raise a further calibration question: whether to fit one global calibration map or many population-specific ones, per station, per time-of-day regime, trading statistical efficiency, more data per map, against fidelity to genuinely different subpopulations whose true score-to-frequency relationship may differ. An open research question is how to calibrate scores from models that themselves change frequently, since a model retrained weekly needs its calibration map refit in lockstep, and doing that reliably and automatically, without a human in the loop each time, is still mostly solved by careful pipeline engineering rather than a general algorithmic answer.

distribution.def: How often each possible value of a quantity occurs, described as a shape, a histogram, or a set of probabilities.
levels: If you dumped out a big bag of different-colored candies and counted how many of each color, that count is a distribution, since it tells you which colors show up a lot and which barely show up at all.

A distribution describes how spread out or clustered a bunch of values are, which values happen a lot, which happen rarely, and everything in between. If you plotted every 5-minute speed reading from one freeway station on a chart, the tall bars around 65 mph and the short bars near 20 mph would show you the speed distribution at that station.
